title: In the Beginning: God Makes the World
summary: God speaks the world into being over six days, bringing order out of what was formless and empty and filling it with light, sky, sea, land, plants, and living creatures. On the sixth day he makes human beings in his own image, male and female, blesses them, and gives them the earth to fill and rule. He looks at everything he has made and calls it very good.
story: This is where the whole story starts, and it starts with God rather than with us. Before there is a people, a law, or a temple, there is a maker and a world he calls good. Everything that follows in the Bible assumes this chapter. The fall in Genesis 3 is tragic because the world was good; the rescue that runs from Abraham to Jesus is a rescue of this world, not an escape from it; and the Bible's last pages describe a new heaven and a new earth, the first creation healed and completed. When you read about exile and return, kingdom and temple, cross and resurrection, keep this chapter in mind. It is what God is getting back.
historical:
Genesis doesn't tell us when it was written, and the question is debated. Jewish and Christian tradition credits Moses with the first five books of the Bible (the Torah, or Pentateuch), which would place their origin in the second half of the second millennium BC. Many modern scholars see the Pentateuch as gathered and edited over centuries, with Genesis 1 often assigned to a priestly writer during or after the Babylonian exile in the sixth century BC. Others argue for older material and a much earlier core. Readers across these views agree on the chapter's setting in the ancient Near East, the world of Egypt, Canaan, and Mesopotamia, whose peoples had their own accounts of how the world began.

The best known of those accounts is the Babylonian epic Enuma Elish, preserved on clay tablets from the first millennium BC. In it the god Marduk defeats the sea goddess Tiamat in battle, splits her body to form the sky and the earth, and has humanity made from the blood of a slain rebel god so that people can do the gods' work for them. Egyptian texts describe creation rising out of primeval waters. Genesis 1 shares some of the furniture of that world (waters, an expanse above, the separation of realms) but tells a very different story, and the differences are the point.
cultural:
An ancient reader would notice at once what is missing. There is no battle. The deep and the great sea creatures, which neighboring peoples feared as chaos powers or gods, are simply things God made. The sun and moon, worshiped across the ancient world, aren't even named; they are called the greater light and the lesser light, lamps hung in the sky to mark days, seasons, and years. The Hebrew word for sun was also the name of a sun god, and the text quietly declines to use it. Nothing in the created world is divine.

The making of humanity would have startled that reader most. Kings in the ancient Near East set up statues of themselves in the lands they ruled, as the visible sign of their authority there, and some kings were called the image of a god. Genesis gives that title to every human being, male and female alike. People are not slaves made to feed the gods, as in the Babylonian story. They are God's royal representatives, blessed and given work: to fill the earth, cultivate it, and rule it on his behalf. The seven-day pattern, which continues into Genesis 2:1-3, also gave Israel the shape of its week and its Sabbath rest.
literary: Genesis 1 is carefully built, closer to a hymn or a liturgy than to a lab report. Refrains repeat: "And God said", "And it was so", "God saw that it was good", and "there was evening, and there was morning". Verse 2 names two problems, the earth "formless and void", and the days answer them in order. Days one to three form realms (light and dark, sky and sea, dry land), and days four to six fill those same realms (lights, birds and fish, animals and people). Day one pairs with day four, two with five, and three with six. The climax is the sixth day, where the rhythm slows and the verse breaks into poetry: "So God created man in His own image; in the image of God He created him; male and female He created them."

outline.t: God, the beginning, and a world formless and empty
Day two: the sky separates the waters
Day three: land, seas, and plants
Day four: sun, moon, and stars
Day five: sea creatures and birds
Day six: humanity in God's image, blessed and given work

doctrines.note: God alone creates, by his word, and the world is good because he made it. Nothing in creation is a god, and nothing in it is evil by nature. The church later expressed this as creation from nothing: God did not shape pre-existing stuff that rivaled him.

Every human being, male and female, bears the image of God. This is the Bible's foundation for human dignity, and it comes before any mention of nation, ability, or achievement. The calling to fill and rule the earth is stewardship under God, not license to exploit.

The chapter shows who God is before it says anything about us: sovereign, orderly, generous, and delighted with what he has made. He speaks, and it is done. Christians have also noticed the Spirit hovering in verse 2 and the "Us" of verse 26, which they read in light of the Trinity, though most scholars think the first readers heard a plural of majesty or God speaking to his heavenly court.

words.note: Bara, to create. In the Hebrew Bible this verb only ever has God as its subject; people make and build, but only God creates. It appears at the three decisive points of the chapter: the heavens and the earth (verse 1), the great sea creatures and living things (verse 21), and humanity (verse 27, three times). The word itself doesn't prove creation from nothing, but it marks acts that belong to God alone.

Tselem, image. Elsewhere in the Old Testament the word is used for statues, including idols. That background is the key: an image stands in a place to represent someone who rules there. Humans are God's living images in his world. It also explains the later ban on carved images of God, since he has already placed his image on earth, in people.

Yom, day. Usually a normal day, but the word has a range: in Genesis 2:4 it covers the whole creation week ("in the day that the LORD God made them"). How to read the days is one of the chapter's great debates, set out under the hard question below.

christ: The New Testament reads this chapter as the first act of a story that Christ completes. John's Gospel opens with the same words, "In the beginning", and says that the Word who was with God and was God is the one through whom all things were made (John 1:1-3). Paul calls Christ "the image of the invisible God" and says all things were created through him and for him (Colossians 1:15-16). Where Adam was made in God's image to rule the world well and failed, Jesus is the true image who rules as a servant. And the light that God speaks into darkness on the first day becomes Paul's picture of salvation: the God who said let light shine out of darkness has shone in our hearts in the face of Christ (2 Corinthians 4:6). None of this is hidden code in Genesis 1; it is the later story showing where the first one was going.

hard.q: Are these six literal days, and can Genesis 1 be squared with modern science?
hard.a:
Christians who share the same confession about God as creator read the days in several ways. The young-earth view takes them as six ordinary 24-hour days a few thousand years ago and reads the rest of Scripture's genealogies the same way. The day-age view takes each day as a long period, since the word can mean an age. The framework view notes the matching of days one to three with four to six and argues that the week is a literary structure arranging God's works topically rather than chronologically. The analogical-days view (associated with C. John Collins) sees God's workweek as the pattern for ours, with days that are God's days, not necessarily 24-hour ones. The cosmic-temple view (argued by John Walton in The Lost World of Genesis One, 2009) reads the chapter as God inaugurating the world as his temple, assigning functions rather than describing material origins. Questions about the days are older than modern science: Augustine, in the early fifth century, already argued that God's creation need not have taken six ordinary days.

What the chapter plainly teaches, on every one of these readings, is who made the world, what it is for, and who we are in it. That is the church's first-order confession. How long it took is a second-order question on which faithful readers differ.

questions: What does it change about how you see a stranger, an enemy, or yourself to believe that every person bears the image of God?
The chapter calls the physical world good, and very good. Where do you tend to treat the body, work, or the created world as less spiritual than it is?
Neighboring peoples feared the sea and worshiped the sun. What powers do people fear or trust today that Genesis 1 would call mere creatures?
